<!-- TODO(Sara): placement. Drafted as its own page next to the socioeconomic variables, because SEPLINE treats ethnicity as a related factor and that page does not implement it. It could instead be a section there. -->

Use this page if your study needs to describe or adjust for immigrant status or
country of origin. The registers do not hold ethnicity. They hold what the Civil
Registration System (CPR) records about birthplace and citizenship, for the
person and for the parents, and Statistics Denmark (DST) derives groups from
that. This page says how DST defines the groups and what to check before you use
them. <!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->

SEPLINE, the national guideline behind the [socioeconomic
variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#sepline-in-brief), says the same: country
of origin and immigration status are an attempt to approximate ethnic minority
status, not ethnicity itself ([Hjorth et al.
2025](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772), section on ethnicity).

## Where the variables are {#variables}

| Information | Register | Variables | From |
| ----------- | -------- | --------- | ---- |
| Person of Danish origin, immigrant or descendant | BEF | `ie_type` | 1985 |
| Country of origin | BEF | `opr_land` | 1985 |
| Date, direction and country of each migration | VNDS | `haend_dato`, `indud_kode`, `indud_land` | 1973 |
| First and latest immigration | BEF | `foerste_indvandring`, `seneste_indvandring` | 2004 |
| Months of residence in Denmark | BEF | `opholdmd_dk` | 1985 |
| Ground of residence, for example refugee | OPHG | `kategori`, `grundlag`, `forklar` | 1997 |

BEF is the population register and VNDS the migration register. DST closed
VNDS in February 2026 and split it into `VNDS_ind`, `VNDS_ud` and `VNDS_hist`;
see the [register reference](register-reference.qmd) for which one you have.
Sources: [Hjorth et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772), Table 13,
and [DST's variable list for
BEF](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/BEF%20-%20Befolkningen.html).
SEPLINE gives 2004 for all three BEF migration columns, but DST's variable list
has `opholdmd_dk` from 1985. Column lists for BEF and VNDS are in the [register
reference](register-reference.qmd).

## Immigrant, descendant or Danish origin (`ie_type`) {#ie-type}

DST's definitions, from its documentation of
[IE_TYPE](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/generelt-om-data/dokumentation-af-data/hoejkvalitetsvariable/Udlaendinge/IE-TYPE):

| Code | Group | DST's wording, and a translation |
| ---- | ----- | -------------------------------- |
| 1 | Persons of Danish origin | "Personer med dansk oprindelse er personer - uanset fødested - der har mindst én forælder, der både er dansk statsborger og født i Danmark." At least one parent is both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark, wherever the person was born. |
| 2 | Immigrants | "Indvandrere er født i udlandet. Ingen af forældrene er både danske statsborgere og født i Danmark." Born abroad, and no parent is both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark. |
| 3 | Descendants | Born in Denmark, and no parent is both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark. |
| 9 | Not stated (uoplyst) | |

The codes and labels are in DST's classification [Herkomst,
v1:1980](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/nomenklaturer/herkomst),
valid from 1 January 1980 and still valid. DST's high-quality page lists "uoplyst" as
`0`, not `9`, so run `count(ie_type)` on your own delivery.

When no parent is known, DST uses the person's own information: "Hvis der ikke
findes oplysninger om nogen af forældrene, og personen er født i udlandet,
opfattes personen også som indvandrer." A person with no known parent who is a
foreign citizen is a descendant, and a person with no known parent who was born
in Denmark is of Danish origin.

## Country of origin (`opr_land`) {#opr-land}

`opr_land` is a country code, and it is not the country of birth. DST defines
it from birth country and citizenship country by these rules ([DST,
OPR_LAND](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/Times/cpr-oplysninger/opr-land)):

- A person of Danish origin always has Denmark.
- If no parent is known, the origin is taken from the person's own information.
  For an immigrant it is the country of birth, for a descendant the country of
  citizenship.
- If only one parent is known, it is that parent's country of birth, or the
  parent's country of citizenship if the parent was born in Denmark.
- If both parents are known, it is the mother's country of birth, or her country
  of citizenship if she was born in Denmark.

So a descendant's country of origin follows the parents, not the place where the
descendant was born. DST's definition does not tell you whether one of the
parents was born in Denmark. SEPLINE suggests a separate group for people of
Danish origin with one parent born in Denmark and one parent born abroad (Table
14 in [Hjorth et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772)). The parents
are found through `mor_id` and `far_id` in BEF. A parent's `opr_land` does not
give that parent's birthplace: by the rules above, a parent born abroad to a
Danish-born Danish citizen is of Danish origin and has Denmark.

Some codes are not current countries. DST lists former states such as the Soviet
Union, which appear when a person is still recorded in CPR with that country,
and areas such as Palestine (5157), Gaza (5223), the West Bank (5393) and East
Jerusalem (5437). A number of codes were retired and folded into others, for
example East Germany (5184) into Germany (5180) on 3 October 1990. Group through DST's
classification below rather than by hand, and check with `anti_join()` that
every code in your data gets a group.

## Western and non-Western, and other country groupings {#groupings}

DST publishes country codes in the classification [Lande i
personstatistik,
v1:2021](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/nomenklaturer/lande-psd),
valid from 1 January 2021. It has three groupings.

| Grouping | Groups |
| -------- | ------ |
| Vestlige/Ikke-vestlige lande (Western and non-Western countries) | Denmark, Western countries, non-Western countries, unknown |
| EU/EØS-lande (EU/EEA and countries outside the EU/EEA) | EU/EEA, outside the EU/EEA |
| World regions (the default hierarchy) | Europe, Africa, America, Asia, Oceania, stateless and unknown, with subgroups such as EU-27 without the United Kingdom |

DST's classification lists the Western countries and gives no definition. They
are the EU countries, the United Kingdom, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein,
Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the Vatican, Canada, the USA, Australia
and New Zealand. Denmark, the Faroe Islands and Greenland form a group of their
own. The United Kingdom is Western and not in the EU/EEA group, so the two
groupings are not the same. In the EU/EEA grouping, Denmark, the Faroe Islands
and Greenland sit inside the EU/EEA group, so set people of Danish origin apart
with `ie_type` first if you compare EU/EEA with the rest.

DST has used the Western and non-Western grouping since 2002. In 2019 DST
concluded that it "fortsat er anvendelig til statistiske opgørelser" and kept
it. One reason is that it is written into current legislation. DST describes the
aim as groups that differ as much as possible from each other and are fairly
uniform within, not groups by culture, and notes that Japan is non-Western. At
the same time DST added the EU/EEA grouping, and 93.4 percent of Western
immigrants and descendants fall in the EU/EEA group ([Elmeskov, DST, 11 July
2019](https://www.dst.dk/da/presse/rigsstat-klumme/2019/2019-07-11-derfor-inddeler-vi-verden-i-vestlige-og-ikke-vestlige-lande)).

SEPLINE gives Western and non-Western as one possible split, lists world regions
and EU/EEA against the rest as the alternatives from DST, and recommends the
most detailed reporting the data allow. If you build your own regional
grouping, define it in the methods.

## Migration type and arrival {#migration}

Which register holds the migration events, and how to use them to decide residence
on an index date, are covered in
[Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd#step-1) and in the [VNDS section of the
register reference](register-reference.qmd).

For the reason for migration, the registers say little. The ground of residence
in OPHG is registered from 1997 and can be used to identify refugees. Before
1997 there is a register at DST with mainly imputed values, which SEPLINE does
not recommend for small study populations. Some studies approximate refugee
status by country of origin and arrival in 1986 to 1992 ([Hjorth et al.
2025](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772), section on ethnicity). Length of
stay can be calculated from the migration events or taken from
`opholdmd_dk` in BEF from 1985.

## Limitations {#limitations}

- **Status can change.** A descendant whose Danish-born parents both keep a
  foreign citizenship stays a descendant. If one of them becomes a Danish
  citizen, DST classifies the child as of Danish origin, and the country of
  origin changes with it. Decide the date at which you fix the status, and
  report it.
- **Before 2008, one status per year.** SEPLINE states that before 2008
  `ie_type` and `opr_land` are only available for people who lived in Denmark
  the whole calendar year. DST's page for IE_TYPE describes the population as
  people with permanent residence in Denmark on 1 January of the year (our
  translation). Newly registered residents and people without a
  Danish CPR number, such as asylum seekers, are missing. After 2008 the
  information is quarterly. SEPLINE suggests using a nearby year if the index
  year is missing ([Hjorth et al.
  2025](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772)).
- **Event tables from the second quarter of 2019.** In DST's event tables, such
  as births, deaths and migrations, `ie_type` and `opr_land` are formed on the
  event date and not at the end of the quarter.
- **No history before arrival.** Births, diagnoses and education abroad are not
  in the Danish registers. For education, see how [missing education is
  handled](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#education). A sensitivity analysis
  restricted to people born in Denmark reduces the problem for your outcome, but
  it also removes the immigrants, who may be the group your question is about.
- **Not a measure of ethnicity.** The definitions depend on citizenship and
  birthplace, and they say nothing about how a person identifies. SEPLINE adds
  that these variables proxy many other circumstances and are often mediators
  of socioeconomic differences, not confounders.
- **Emigration.** People leave and return. Use the migration events to censor at
  emigration, see [Attach date of death and emigration](joins.qmd#death-emigration).

## Count the groups in your cohort {#count}

Check by eye on your own data before you build on it. The sketch reads the most
recent BEF snapshot up to the year before index, the same baseline year as the
[socioeconomic recipes](socioeconomic-variables.qmd), so the status is fixed
before follow-up starts. It keeps unknown as its own category, as on the
[socioeconomic variables page](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#missing), and keeps
people with no BEF row in that period apart from DST's own unknown.

```r
library(dplyr) # select, collect, inner_join, filter, arrange, distinct, left_join, mutate, count
library(lubridate) # year
library(fastreg) # read_register

# BEF, lazily; lower-case column names
bef <- read_register("bef") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)

# One row per cohort row: the newest BEF snapshot up to the year before index
# (year_baseline, as in the socioeconomic recipes). If your BEF holds several
# snapshots per year, keep the December one first, as under "Check your BEF"
# on the socioeconomic variables page.
origin <- bef %>%
  select(pnr, year, ie_type, opr_land) %>%
  # only the cohort's pnr, filtered in the database: BEF for the whole
  # population over many years is too large to collect
  semi_join(distinct(cohort, pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  collect() %>%
  inner_join(
    cohort %>% mutate(year_baseline = year(index_date) - 1) %>% select(row_id, pnr, year_baseline),
    by = "pnr",
    relationship = "many-to-many" # a pnr can have several snapshots AND several cohort rows
  ) %>%
  filter(year <= year_baseline) %>%
  arrange(row_id, desc(year)) %>%
  distinct(row_id, .keep_all = TRUE) # newest snapshot per cohort row

cohort <- cohort %>%
  left_join(select(origin, row_id, ie_type, opr_land), by = "row_id") %>%
  mutate(
    origin_group = case_when(
      !row_id %in% origin$row_id ~ "Not in BEF", # no snapshot up to the baseline year
      ie_type == 1 ~ "Danish origin",
      ie_type == 2 ~ "Immigrant",
      ie_type == 3 ~ "Descendant",
      TRUE ~ "Missing" # DST's own unknown code, or no value
    )
  )

stopifnot(nrow(cohort) == n_distinct(cohort$row_id)) # nobody lost or duplicated
count(cohort, origin_group)
```

To split into Western and non-Western, join `opr_land` to DST's country
classification above. Do not type the list of countries by hand.
